# Unsigned Time Arithmetic and Rollover

A millisecond counter in a fixed-width unsigned type wraps to zero. On a 32-bit `millis()`
that happens after **49.7 days**. Whether the wrap is harmless or fatal is decided by one
line of arithmetic.

```cpp
if (now - then >= interval)          // correct through the rollover
if (now > then + interval)           // fails at the rollover
```

## Why the subtraction form survives

Unsigned arithmetic in C and C++ is defined to wrap modulo 2ⁿ. So when `now` has wrapped
and `then` has not, `now - then` *also* wraps — and comes out as the true elapsed
interval, not as an enormous number. The overflow in the subtraction cancels the overflow
in the clock.

The addition form has no such symmetry. `then + interval` overflows to a small number, the
comparison `now > small` becomes true immediately or stays false for weeks depending on
where the wrap fell, and the scheduler either fires continuously or never fires again.

The rule is worth stating positively, because it generalises past clocks: **compare
differences, not sums.** Any monotonically increasing counter in a bounded type — sequence
numbers, tick counters, byte offsets — behaves the same way.

## Why it is almost never caught

The reproduction time is 49.7 days of continuous uptime. No test suite waits for it, no lab
demonstration reaches it, and no code review notices it, because the wrong form is the one
that reads more naturally in English: *"if now is past then-plus-the-interval"*.

It is therefore a defect discovered exclusively in deployed systems, months after the
person who wrote it moved on. That profile — invisible to every check that exists, correct
in every observation anyone makes — is the same one that makes
[[tests-that-pass-for-the-wrong-reason]] worth its own page.

The fix in a test suite is not to wait. It is to make the clock a parameter, so a test can
hand the state machine a timestamp near the wrap boundary and assert the transition. That
is available only if the logic was lifted out of `loop()` first — see
[[separating-computation-from-io]].

## The related trap: blocking instead of scheduling

`delay()` is not a timing primitive; it is a promise that nothing else happens. A "blink"
implemented with `delay()` drops serial input and freezes display refreshes for its
duration, on a controller with no other thread to pick up the slack. Timestamp-driven
scheduling — record `then`, return, and check the difference on the next pass — is what
makes several timed behaviours coexist in one loop.
